title: Lessons From My Master of Education Research About Note-Taking in High School
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson looks back at a six-week applied research project from his 2023 Master of Education, in which he combined digital note-taking and reflective journaling with six secondary students in Surabaya, Indonesia. He began from a familiar classroom problem: students learned new things daily but he was not convinced it stuck. Mean assessment scores rose from 54 percent to 92 percent, and students reported feeling more organized and confident, yet reflective journaling landed unevenly and some barely completed it. Hutson is candid about the limits, noting the tiny sample, the lack of a control group and his dual role as teacher and researcher, and says the original paper overstated its conclusions. His main lesson is that a note's value begins after it is written, when the learner interprets it, finds gaps and returns to it later. He closes with a five-step routine for giving notes a second life and ties the work to his CARE teaching method.
points: Taking notes is not the same as learning, because a full notebook can preserve information without changing understanding.
Reflective note-taking adds the questions of what the information means, how it connects to prior knowledge and what to do with it.
Strong score gains in a six-student study with no control group cannot be attributed to the intervention, and Hutson says so plainly.
Students will not value reflective journaling unless they are taught why reflection matters, not just how to do it.
A simple routine of capturing, interpreting, noting gaps, returning later and applying an idea gives notes a second life.
quotes: My students learned new things every day, but I wasn’t convinced that the learning was sticking.
But a notebook full of information doesn’t necessarily show what the person understands.
Traditional note-taking asks: What information should I remember? Reflective note-taking adds: What does this information mean to me, how does it connect to what I know, and what might I do with it?
This was a small applied research project, not a large controlled experiment. It involved only six students, all from the same educational setting.
The results were encouraging, but they were not proof that a six-week note-taking program caused students’ grades to improve.
But familiarity with a strategy is not the same as understanding its purpose.
What makes a note valuable is the intellectual work that develops around it.
Don’t consider a note finished simply because you’ve written it down. Give it another opportunity to develop.
